### Three Ages of AI in Science

To understand where we are, it helps to understand how we got here. The history of AI in scientific research can be divided into three distinct eras, each defined by a qualitative shift in the relationship between the AI system and the human researcher. Maya's own career, spanning the mid-2010s to the present, runs neatly through all three.

**The Pre-LLM Era (before 2023): AI as Specialized Instrument.** In this era, machine learning models served as precision instruments for specific prediction tasks within the scientific workflow. AlphaFold predicted protein structures from amino acid sequences. Graph neural networks predicted molecular properties. Random forests classified cell types from single-cell RNA sequencing data. These tools were powerful (AlphaFold's impact on structural biology was genuinely revolutionary), but they operated within tight boundaries. A researcher needed to do four things: (a) know the tool existed; (b) format their data into the tool's expected input; (c) interpret the output in the context of their research question; and (d) decide what to do next based on the results. The AI did one thing superbly; the researcher did everything else.

For Maya's drug repurposing problem, this era offered molecular docking software (to predict whether a drug molecule would bind to a target protein), network analysis tools (to model disease pathways), and statistical packages (to identify differentially expressed genes). Each tool accelerated a single step. Nothing connected the steps or made decisions about which steps to take.

**The Tool-Augmented LLM Era (2023): AI as Versatile Assistant.** The release of GPT-4 in March 2023 changed the field dramatically, not because the model itself could do science, but because it could *use tools* through natural language instructions. ChemCrow ([Bran et al., Nature MI 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.05376)), released in April 2023, was a landmark demonstration: researchers at EPFL and the University of Rochester gave GPT-4 access to eighteen expert chemistry tools for name-to-SMILES conversion (translating a drug name into its molecular structure), molecular property prediction, reaction feasibility checking, safety hazard lookup, and synthesis route planning. The system successfully designed novel chromophores and planned synthesis routes, earning publication in *Nature Machine Intelligence*.

What made ChemCrow significant was not any single capability (each tool pre-existed) but the *integration*: the LLM served as a general-purpose reasoning engine that could decide *which* tool to use, *when* to use it, and *how* to interpret the result in context. For Maya, this era brought tools like ChatGPT-based brainstorming for hypotheses, Copilot-assisted coding for analysis scripts, and GPT-4-powered literature search assistants. She used them daily, and they saved hours of work. But she still drove the process: she decided which questions to ask, which analyses to run, and how to interpret the results.

**The Agentic Era (2024-2025): AI as Semi-Autonomous Researcher.** The transition from the tool-augmented era to the agentic era was not a single breakthrough but a convergence of capabilities. In late 2023, Coscientist ([Boiko et al., Nature 2023](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06792-0)) demonstrated that an LLM could not just *plan* but *execute* chemistry experiments through robotic lab APIs. In early 2024, ResearchAgent ([Baek et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07738)) showed that LLMs could iteratively refine research hypotheses through simulated peer review. By mid-2024, The AI Scientist ([Lu et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.06292)) had demonstrated the full loop, from idea to paper, without human intervention. And by 2025, multi-agent systems like Robin and Google's AI co-scientist were generating hypotheses that were being validated in real laboratories.

The defining characteristic of this era is *agency*: the AI system makes decisions about what to investigate, how to investigate it, and when to pivot based on results. The human role shifts from driver to supervisor, from author to editor, from experimenter to auditor.

::: {.callout-note title="Think Hard: What does 'autonomous' actually mean here?"}
When we say a system operates "autonomously," the word hides important subtlety. Coscientist autonomously executes chemistry experiments, but only within the narrow space of Suzuki coupling reactions, using pre-configured cloud lab equipment, with a human having pre-selected the reaction type. The AI Scientist autonomously writes papers, but only starting from human-crafted code templates (in v1) or within narrowly scoped ML topic areas (v2). Robin autonomously discovers drug candidates, but within the specific protocol of drug repurposing, using databases curated by human biologists. Every "autonomous" system operates within a *sandbox* defined by human designers. The question is not whether the system is truly autonomous (none are), but how large and well-defined the sandbox is, and whether the system can operate reliably within it. The shift from tool to agent is not about removing humans from the loop, but about *changing where humans sit in the loop*: from executing every step to defining the boundaries and reviewing the results.
:::

### The Tool → Analyst → Scientist Taxonomy

The three eras map naturally onto a capability taxonomy proposed in the survey "From Automation to Autonomy" ([Zheng et al., ACL 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13259)), which provides a clean framework for classifying any AI-for-science system. This taxonomy is not about the size of the model or the sophistication of the architecture; it is about the *scope of autonomous decision-making* the system exercises.

**Level 1: Tool.** The AI handles a single, well-defined task within the scientific workflow. The human researcher identifies the problem, designs the experiment, and interprets the results; the AI accelerates one step. Examples:

- Using ChatGPT to brainstorm research questions
- Using Copilot to write analysis code
- Using AlphaFold to predict protein structures
- Using LLM-SR to discover equations from data (when invoked by a human on a specific dataset)

The key signature of Level 1 is that the human makes all *strategic* decisions. The AI makes no choices about what problem to work on, what data to collect, or how to interpret results in context.

**Level 2: Analyst.** The AI manages a multi-step sub-workflow, making tactical decisions within a constrained pipeline. The human defines the overall goal and evaluation criteria; the AI chooses how to achieve them within its operational envelope. Examples:

- DS-Agent: given a Kaggle dataset and a target metric, it autonomously explores the data, selects features, builds models, tunes hyperparameters, and reports results
- LIDA: given a dataset and a natural-language question, it summarizes the data, generates analysis goals, writes visualization code, and creates infographics
- PaperQA2: given a research question, it searches a corpus, retrieves relevant passages, synthesizes an answer with citations, and assesses citation quality
- SELA: given a prediction task, it uses tree-search to explore and optimize ML pipeline configurations

The key signature of Level 2 is *tactical autonomy*: the system makes a sequence of decisions within a known framework, but it cannot redefine the problem itself. DS-Agent will build you the best model it can for predicting housing prices, but it will never suggest that housing prices are the wrong variable to predict.

**Level 3: Scientist.** The AI drives a substantial portion of (or the entire) research cycle, including problem identification, hypothesis generation, experimental design, execution, analysis, and communication. Examples:

- The AI Scientist (v1 and v2): generates research ideas, writes experimental code, runs experiments, creates figures, writes papers, and produces automated reviews
- Robin (FutureHouse): searches literature, generates drug repurposing hypotheses, designs and runs analyses, produces validated candidates
- Google AI Co-Scientist: generates hypotheses, debates them across multiple agents, refines survivors, produces validated predictions

The key signature of Level 3 is *strategic autonomy*: the system chooses *what* to investigate, not just *how*. This is also where the most dramatic failures occur, because strategic decisions require the kind of scientific judgment that current LLMs struggle with most: distinguishing important problems from trivial ones, recognizing when a result is "too good to be true," and understanding the context that makes a finding significant.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common Misconception: Higher levels are always better"}
It is tempting to view this taxonomy as a ladder where Level 3 is the goal and Levels 1 and 2 are mere stepping stones. This framing is misleading. For many practical research scenarios, a Level 2 system that reliably automates data analysis (like DS-Agent, which achieves 100% task completion with GPT-4 on Kaggle datasets) is far more useful than a Level 3 system that attempts the full research cycle but succeeds only 25-34% of the time (as benchmarks show). The right level depends on the task, the risk tolerance, and the value of human judgment in the loop. Maya does not need an AI that replaces her. She needs an AI that saves her six months on literature review while she applies her irreplaceable domain expertise to evaluating the hypotheses.
:::

### Architectural Building Blocks

Regardless of where a system falls on the Tool→Analyst→Scientist spectrum, nearly all AI agents for science share a common architectural pattern drawn from the broader agentic AI research. Understanding these building blocks helps you see the *structural* similarities across systems that superficially look very different.

**Perception** is how the agent takes in information: reading papers (text), interpreting figures and charts (vision), processing experimental data (structured data), and observing the output of code execution (terminal logs). Multimodal LLMs like GPT-4V and Gemini 2.0 have dramatically expanded the perception frontier. Robin's "Falcon" agent, for example, reads and interprets figures from scientific papers as part of its literature review.

**Reasoning** is how the agent decides what to do next. The simplest form is direct prompting ("Given this context, what should the next step be?"). More sophisticated approaches include chain-of-thought reasoning, which breaks a complex decision into explicit intermediate steps, and ReAct-style interleaving of reasoning and action (think, act, observe, think again). At the most structured end, tree-search methods like MCTS systematically explore multiple possible action sequences and select the most promising. The AI Scientist v2's "progressive agentic tree search" is an example of tree-based reasoning applied to the research process itself.

**Action** is how the agent modifies the world: executing Python code (CodeAct), calling external APIs (ChemCrow's tool calls), controlling laboratory equipment (Coscientist's cloud-lab integration), writing documents (AI Scientist's LaTeX paper generation), and searching the web or literature databases (PaperQA2's retrieval).

**Memory** is how the agent retains and retrieves information across the arc of a research project. This includes three forms: short-term memory (the LLM's context window, which holds the current conversation and recent observations), long-term storage (RAG-based systems that retrieve from a knowledge base, like PaperQA2's paper corpus), and structured knowledge (DS-Agent's case-based reasoning library, which stores and retrieves strategies from past Kaggle competitions). Memory is arguably the most underappreciated building block. Many of the performance improvements seen in domain-specific agents come from better memory systems rather than better reasoning.

### Mapping the Current Field

With the taxonomy and building blocks in hand, we can now draw a map of the current field. The figure below organizes the major systems by their primary target in the scientific workflow (x-axis) and their level of autonomy (y-axis). This map reveals two important patterns.

First, there is a clear **diagonal** from lower-left (Level 1 tools targeting single steps) to upper-right (Level 3 systems targeting the full cycle). Most existing systems cluster along this diagonal, suggesting that autonomy level and workflow scope tend to scale together.

Second, there is notable **density at Level 2**, the analyst level, where the most practically successful systems live. DS-Agent, PaperQA2, LIDA, SELA, and ChemCrow are all Level 2 systems that have demonstrated reliable, measurably valuable performance on real-world tasks. The Level 3 systems (AI Scientist, Robin, Google co-scientist) generate the most excitement but are also the most contested. Their successes are dramatic; their failure rates, as we will see in @sec-benchmarks, remain high.

::: {.callout-note title="Think Hard: Why the 'analyst' level is the current sweet spot"}
There is a structural reason why Level 2 systems tend to outperform Level 3 systems on benchmarks. At Level 2, the *problem definition* is provided by a human (or a benchmark), which eliminates the hardest part of research: deciding what question to ask. The agent then operates within a constrained search space where the evaluation criteria are clear and the action space is manageable. At Level 3, the agent must simultaneously solve two problems (deciding what to investigate *and* deciding how to investigate it), where the first problem is open-ended and poorly defined, and errors in the first problem propagate through everything that follows.

This asymmetry mirrors a well-known phenomenon in human research: senior scientists are valued not primarily for their technical skills (which many graduate students share) but for their ability to *choose important problems*. Current Level 3 systems lack precisely this strategic judgment. The implication is that the path to Level 3 may not be simply "scale up Level 2" but may require fundamentally different approaches to problem selection and scientific taste.
:::

**Where Maya fits.** After learning this taxonomy, Maya realizes that her current use of LLMs is solidly Level 1 (brainstorming, coding assistance). She sees that Level 2 tools like PaperQA2 (for literature synthesis) and DS-Agent (for data analysis) could immediately accelerate her work without requiring her to trust an AI with strategic decisions. The Level 3 systems (Robin, Google co-scientist, AI Scientist) are intriguing but not ready for her high-stakes drug repurposing work, where a false positive could waste months of wet-lab validation time. This calibrated assessment, choosing the right autonomy level for the task and risk, is exactly what the taxonomy is designed to enable.
